input: How do n-gram embedding tables compare to traditional embeddings in enhancing language model performance?
actual_output:
The retrieved paper titled "Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models" (arXiv:2610.31646v1) provides insights into the advantages of n-gram embedding tables over traditional embeddings in enhancing language model performance.

1. **Memory Efficiency**: The study demonstrates that low-bit precision n-gram embedding tables can significantly reduce memory usage while maintaining performance. For instance, using four-bit tables can save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the performance improvement provided by full-precision tables (16-bit) (Section 5 Conclusion). This contrasts with traditional embeddings, which typically do not offer such efficient memory savings.

2. **Performance Retention**: The paper highlights that n-gram embeddings, particularly when compressed to low-bit representations, retain a substantial portion of their performance benefits. For example, while two-bit tables save 86-87% of table memory, they still retain 85.9-91.0% of the original improvement compared to models without n-gram tables (Section 3.2). This suggests that n-gram embeddings are more resilient to precision reduction than traditional embeddings.

3. **Joint Learning**: N-gram embedding tables are learned jointly with the language model, which allows them to capture contextual patterns more effectively than traditional embeddings that may not leverage such contextual information (Section 2 Method). The paper indicates that using multiple embedding tables for bigrams and trigrams enhances language modeling performance, with further gains as the number of embeddings increases.

4. **Component-wise Hashing**: The paper also explores alternative hashing methods for n-gram embeddings, such as same-column and fully random component hashing, which improve performance at low precision compared to conventional whole-embedding hashing. This flexibility in parameter sharing allows n-grams to maintain performance even when using lower precision, which is not typically a feature of traditional embeddings (Section C.6).

In summary, n-gram embedding tables provide significant advantages over traditional embeddings in terms of memory efficiency, performance retention under compression, and the ability to learn contextual patterns effectively. These findings suggest that n-gram embeddings are a valuable enhancement for language models, particularly in scenarios where memory resources are constrained.
expected_output: N-gram embedding tables enhance language model performance by storing learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. This approach allows models to retrieve relevant embeddings during processing, adding substantial capacity with minimal computational overhead. In contrast, traditional embeddings typically represent individual tokens without capturing their contextual relationships as effectively. Studies show that n-gram tables can significantly improve performance, with low-bit precision methods preserving most of these benefits while reducing memory costs. For instance, three-bit n-gram tables can save approximately 75% of table memory while retaining over 99% of the validation-loss improvement compared to models without n-gram embeddings.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 5 Conclusion

We propose low-bit precision for n-gram embedding tables and systematically study its effects on memory use and model performance. Across models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables. Choosing appropriate embedding scales matters more than the choice of codebook, and mixed precision allows different n-gram tables to use the precision they need. At lower precision, a brief fine-tuning phase can recover much of the lost performance. These findings also extend to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, where compression saves 47-55% of table memory with little change in perplexity and downstream performance. Beyond reducing memory use, reinvesting the savings in more embeddings can improve performance over the original full-precision tables. Together, our results offer practical guidance for making n-gram memory more efficient and using the saved capacity to build better language models.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 2 Method

N-gram embedding tables. Following the Over-Tokenized Transformer [1], we use four embedding tables: two for bigrams and two for trigrams, as illustrated in Figure 1. The embeddings in these tables are learned jointly with the language model, with one embedding stored in each row. At each token position, the bigram and trigram ending at the current token each retrieve one embedding from each of their two corresponding tables. These four embeddings are then concatenated and added to the token embedding. Previous work has shown that this method improves language modeling performance, with further gains as the number of embeddings increases [1].

Formally, let x t denote the current token, E the token embedding matrix with embedding dimension d , and T 1 , . . . , T 4 the four tables. We construct the model input as
where n 1 = n 2 = 2 for the bigram tables and n 3 = n 4 = 3 for the trigram tables. Here, the hash function h j determines which embedding is retrieved by mapping the token sequence to an address in table T j . These retrieved embeddings each have dimension d/ 4, so concatenating all four gives the same dimension as E [ x t ].
Low-bit embeddings. We propose reducing the memory cost of these trained tables by storing their embeddings at low precision. To do this, we give each table a set of up to 2 b representative values, commonly called a codebook , and represent each embedding component by a b -bit index into these shared codebook values. To account for differences in magnitude between embeddings, we also store one 16-bit scale per embedding. During reconstruction, the index selects a codebook value, which is then multiplied by the embedding's scale. Thus, the original component w ri at position i of embedding r is reconstructed as
where s r is the scale, c k is codebook value k , and q ri is the stored index (Figure 1b).
This low-bit representation substantially reduces table memory. For an embedding with p components, memory use falls from 16 p bits to pb + 16 bits. For instance, with p = 128, two-bit precision reduces the memory required per embedding by approximately 87%, from 2,048 to 272 bits.
However, bigram and trigram embeddings represent different context patterns, so they may need different precision to preserve their contribution to model performance. We therefore propose using a mixture of bit widths across the two n-gram orders, allocating more bits to the tables that are more sensitive to quantization within a fixed table memory budget.
Choosing the codebook values. We consider three codebook families. First, uniform codebooks use equally spaced values. For instance, at two bits, the codebook values are {-1 , -1 / 3 , 1 / 3 , 1 } . We also test a variant that includes zero, using {-1 , 0 , 1 } , so that zero can be represented exactly. Second, normal-quantile codebooks take values from quantiles of a standard normal distribution, placing more of them near zero. Third, we learn the codebook values from each table's trained embeddings using Lloyd-Max quantization [4, 5].
To learn the Lloyd-Max codebook, we first normalize each embedding by its root mean square, allowing embeddings of different magnitudes to share a codebook. We initialize the codebook values at quantiles of the normalized components, then repeatedly assign components to their nearest codebook value and replace each value with the mean of its assigned components. This fitting runs once during compression, using only the trained embeddings. Appendix A.2 gives the implementation details.
Choosing the embedding scales. Once the codebook values are fixed, we consider three ways to choose each embedding's scale s r . First, maximum-based scaling matches the largest absolute codebook value to the embedding's largest absolute component. Second, root-mean-square (RMS) scaling uses the embedding's overall magnitude, calculated as s r = √ 1 p ∑ i w 2 ri . Third, error-fitted scaling chooses the scale to minimize the mean squared error between the original embedding and its reconstruction. We compare these choices to examine how scale selection affects compression quality.
After determining the codebook values and embedding scales, we store them together with the low-bit indices in place of the original embedding tables. During inference, the model retrieves embeddings from this stored representation without repeating the fitting procedure.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: C.6 Alternative hashing methods

To examine whether the way n-grams share embedding parameters affects low-bit performance, we compare conventional whole-embedding hashing with two component-wise alternatives. Conventional hashing maps an n-gram to one embedding in each table and retrieves all its components together. Consequently, two n-grams mapped to the same embedding share every component. The alternatives instead choose a separate address for each output component while keeping the same table size and embedding dimension.
Same-column hashing. We retain the table as a matrix, with one embedding per row and one component per column. To construct component j of an n-gram embedding, we hash the n-gram together with j to choose a row, then retrieve the value in column j of that row. Different components can therefore come from different embeddings, but the first component always comes from the first column, the second from the second column, and so on.
Fully random component hashing. We flatten the same table into a vector and hash the n-gram together with each component index to select a value anywhere in that vector. Unlike same-column hashing, the selected value can come from any column as well as any row. In both variants, the hash addresses are fixed: the same n-gram always retrieves the same components, whose values are learned during training.
Experimental setup. We compare all three methods on nanochat 26M, GPT-2-family 30M, and Llamafamily 31M, using the default 262k embeddings per table, ClimbMix, and three seeds. Each comparison uses the same training setup and evaluates both 16-bit and two-bit tables. The two-bit models use quantized embeddings throughout pre-training, following Appendix B.4. We quantize each table using Lloyd-Max codebooks and error-fitted scales before gathering its components, so each selected component keeps the scale of its source embedding.
Table 10: Alternative hashing methods at 16-bit and two-bit precision. Values give the improvement relative to conventional 16-bit tables (%), reported as mean ± sample standard deviation over three seeds. For every row, 100% denotes the validation-loss reduction from adding conventional 16-bit tables to the corresponding model without tables.
Discussion. Table 10 shows that both component-wise methods improve the average two-bit result over conventional hashing on all three architectures. Their improvement reaches 93.6-100.3% of that provided by conventional 16-bit tables, compared with 87.0-93.7% for conventional two-bit hashing. The gains are larger on GPT-2 and Llama than on nanochat, suggesting that the choice of shared embedding components can help preserve performance at low precision.
Same-column hashing also appears promising beyond low precision. It improves mean performance over conventional hashing in five of the six settings, including two of the three full-precision comparisons. One possible explanation is that component-wise hashing allows n-grams to share individual components without sharing an entire embedding, reducing interference from whole-embedding collisions. These results suggest that same-column hashing may offer broader benefits for language modeling. Establishing how consistently it helps and whether collision patterns explain these gains deserves further investigation beyond the scope of this study, which focuses on low-precision embeddings.

Section: 3.2 Table memory savings and model performance

We first ask how much table memory can be removed before the model loses the benefit of n-gram embeddings. We compress the trained tables to one through four bits using Lloyd-Max codebooks with fitted scales. To test whether larger tables can tolerate the same compression, we also increase the number of embeddings per table from the default 262k to 1M in the 26M nanochat model and both Llama-family models.
The results are shown in Figure 2. We find that low-bit compression retains most of the improvement at three or four bits. For example, four-bit tables save 74-75% of table memory while retaining more than 99% of the original improvement. However, reducing precision further hurts performance. Two-bit tables save 86-87% of table memory but retain only 85.9-91.0% of the original improvement. Appendix C gives the full results, including one-bit compression.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 3.1 Experimental setup

Models and data. We train five language models from scratch: nanochat with 26M and 50M parameters, a GPT-2-family model with 30M parameters, and Llama-family models with 31M and 322M parameters. By default, each model uses four n-gram tables, comprising two bigram and two trigram tables, with approximately 262k embeddings per table. We train on ClimbMix [10] and repeat each experiment with three random seeds. Appendix B.1 gives the model configurations and training settings.
Evaluation. For each model, we first train two versions using the same experimental setup, one with fullprecision (16-bit) n-gram tables and one without tables. We evaluate both on a held-out validation dataset, and their difference in validation loss measures the improvement from adding the tables. We then reduce the precision of the trained tables and evaluate the model again to measure how much of this improvement remains. We report this as the percentage of the original improvement retained, where 100% matches the full-precision tables and 0% matches the model trained without tables. Alongside this performance measure, we report the percentage of table memory saved. Results are averaged over three seeds, with standard deviations where shown.

input: How do low-bit n-gram embeddings and full precision compare regarding memory efficiency and performance retention?
actual_output:
Low-bit n-gram embeddings demonstrate significant advantages in memory efficiency compared to full precision embeddings while retaining a substantial portion of performance. According to the findings in "Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models" (arXiv:2610.31646v1), using four-bit tables can save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the performance improvement associated with full-precision tables. This indicates that low-bit embeddings can effectively reduce memory usage without a corresponding significant drop in model performance.

In contrast, as the precision decreases further (e.g., to two bits), while memory savings increase (up to 86-87%), the retention of performance improvement declines, with only 85.9-91.0% of the original improvement being preserved. This suggests that while lower precision can lead to greater memory efficiency, it also risks a more considerable loss in performance (Section 3.2).

Moreover, the research highlights that a brief fine-tuning phase after compressing the n-gram tables can recover much of the lost performance. For instance, after fine-tuning, one-bit and two-bit tables retain 65.3% and 92.0% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables, respectively. Interestingly, one-bit embeddings can perform even better when used throughout pre-training, retaining 77.0% of the full-precision tables' improvement (Section 3.5).

Overall, the findings suggest that low-bit n-gram embeddings offer a practical solution for reducing memory requirements while maintaining a high level of performance, especially when combined with fine-tuning strategies. This approach not only enhances memory efficiency but also allows for the potential reinvestment of saved memory into larger embedding tables, which can further improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables (Abstract).

For instance, three-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while retaining over 99% of the validation-loss improvement from full-precision tables. However, using lower precision can lead to some performance loss. A brief fine-tuning phase after compression can recover much of this loss, with one-bit embeddings retaining 77% of the full-precision improvement when used throughout pre-training. Overall, low-bit embeddings offer a practical way to reduce memory requirements while maintaining performance.

We first ask how much table memory can be removed before the model loses the benefit of n-gram embeddings. We compress the trained tables to one through four bits using Lloyd-Max codebooks with fitted scales. To test whether larger tables can tolerate the same compression, we also increase the number of embeddings per table from the default 262k to 1M in the 26M nanochat model and both Llama-family models.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 3.5 Recovering performance with low-bit training

Compressing the n-gram tables changes the embeddings that the model learned to use, which can reduce performance. We therefore ask whether a short fine-tuning phase can recover this loss, or whether using low-bit embeddings throughout pre-training is more effective. To train with low-bit embeddings, we maintain a BF16 copy for gradient updates but quantize the retrieved embeddings during each forward pass. Both the embeddings and the rest of the model remain trainable, allowing the model to adapt to the chosen precision. We compare four sequences: (1) compress → pre-train, (2) pre-train → compress →fi ne-tune, (3) pre-train → fi ne-tune → compress, and (4) pre-train → compress. Comparing fine-tuning before and after compression tests whether recovery comes from adapting to low-bit embeddings rather than simply receiving more training.
The results are summarized in Figure 6. We observe that a brief fine-tuning phase after compression recovers much of the performance lost at very low precision. After fine-tuning, one- and two-bit tables retain 65.3% and 92.0% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables, respectively. Surprisingly, one-bit embeddings perform even better when used throughout pre-training, retaining 77.0% of the full-precision tables' improvement. This shows that even one bit per embedding component can preserve a large share of the benefit from n-gram tables when the model learns to use them from the start. Appendix C.5 gives the full results, while Appendix C.6 examines how alternative hashing methods affect performance with low-bit embeddings.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.

Section: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Stephen Chung
Wenyu Du

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Section: 1 Introduction

Recent studies have shown that n-gram embedding tables can improve language model performance with little additional computation [1, 2]. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. At each position, the model retrieves the corresponding representations to supplement its processing of the text. Because each lookup accesses only a few embeddings, the tables can add substantial model capacity while keeping the computation per token small. This approach has been adopted in DeepSeek's Engram memory, which contains 196 billion parameters in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [3]. However, storing these large tables requires substantial memory, motivating methods that preserve their performance benefits with a smaller memory footprint.
The memory cost arises from the enormous number of possible token combinations. To accommodate them, existing methods map n-grams into a fixed number of table embeddings, allowing multiple n-grams to share the same embedding [1, 2]. Smaller tables force more unrelated sequences to share representations, which can reduce their benefit to the model. Increasing the number of embeddings alleviates this problem but requires more memory. We therefore investigate a different way to reduce table memory: keeping the embeddings while using fewer bits for each embedding value. This also raises an opportunity: if lower precision preserves most of the tables' benefit, the saved memory could support more embeddings and ultimately improve performance.
We propose compressing n-gram embedding tables by storing each value at low precision. At such low precision, the choice of representable values can affect how well the embeddings are preserved. We therefore systematically compare evenly spaced values, values chosen from normal quantiles, and values fitted to the learned embedding distribution using Lloyd-Max quantization [4, 5]. We also examine whether bigram and trigram tables benefit from different precision levels, allowing us to allocate bits according to their sensitivity to compression. Together, these experiments offer practical guidance on choosing quantization methods and bit allocations to balance table memory and model performance.

input: How do rVCs differ from bVCs in agent authentication, specifically in terms of roles, capabilities, and issuance authority?
actual_output:
In the context of agent authentication, rich Verifiable Credentials (rVCs) and basic Verifiable Credentials (bVCs) serve distinct roles, particularly concerning the information they contain and their issuance authority.

1. **Content and Purpose**:
   - **bVCs**: Basic Verifiable Credentials are designed to encode minimal information. They primarily serve to identify an agent as an entity without specifying detailed attributes, roles, capabilities, or authorizations. The issuance of bVCs is restricted to the orchestrator of the security domain, which means they are only issued at the initial deployment of an agent. Their main purpose is to enable freshly-deployed agents to trustfully identify themselves to peers within the same security domain (arXiv:2511.02841v2).
   - **rVCs**: In contrast, rich Verifiable Credentials contain additional identity attributes, including roles, capabilities, and authorizations of an agent. These credentials are obtained through an intra-domain attestation process, where an agent requests rVCs from a designated authority agent within the same security domain. This process involves mutual authentication, where the requesting agent presents its bVCs, and the issuer presents its own rVCs (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

2. **Issuance Authority**:
   - **bVCs** are exclusively issued by the orchestrator of the security domain, which holds its own DID outside the ledger. This means that bVCs are limited to the initial identification of agents and do not provide any further context about the agent's capabilities or roles (arXiv:2511.02841v2).
   - **rVCs**, on the other hand, are issued by designated authority agents within the security domain after a successful attestation process. This allows for a more dynamic and context-sensitive assignment of roles and capabilities, reflecting the agent's operational context and permissions (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

In summary, the key differences between rVCs and bVCs in agent authentication lie in the depth of information they provide and their respective issuance authorities. bVCs are basic identifiers issued by the orchestrator, while rVCs are richer credentials that convey detailed attributes and are issued through a mutual authentication process involving designated authority agents.
expected_output: rVCs (rich Verifiable Credentials) differ from bVCs (basic Verifiable Credentials) in that rVCs specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent, while bVCs only encode minimal information, primarily confirming that the entity is an agent without detailing its specific roles or capabilities. rVCs are issued by a designated authority agent within the same security domain, whereas bVCs are solely issued by the security domain's orchestrator. This distinction allows agents with rVCs to engage in more complex interactions and trust relationships compared to those with only bVCs.

VCs are explicitly allowed to carry claims in the form of unstructured data such as natural language text, images, or audio. Since modern LLM-based AI agents are able to produce and interpret unstructured content, they can issue and verify unstructured, schemaless claims about other agents. These novel types of claims can bootstrap automated and dynamic trust establishment in multi-agent and cross-domain ecosystems, as different domains do not need to go through an extensive standardization process to reach an agreement on a common rigid VC schema.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 4 Concept Within our concept, each agent lives in the realm of a security domain and is in control of its own DID and VCs. All agents of a security domain are deployed by a dedicated orchestrator. Each agent's DID is anchored in a jointly operated distributed ledger that spans multiple security domains. The ledger is considered to be commonly governed by participants originating from different security domains. It acts as a cross-domain trust anchor for DID docs. Only the agent in possession of the private key associated with a DID is authorized to update its ledger-anchored DID doc, while all agents of the same or different security domain are only allowed to read it. This design ensures tamper-resistant and cross-domain persistence of an agent's identifier and the associated verification material in the form of public keys. So as per definition, each agent has inherent confidence in the operation of the ledger. For secure handling of the agent DID's private key and the VCs themselves, every agent is equipped with a digital wallet. When initiating a dialogue, agents must mutually authenticate, regardless of whether they belong to the same or different security domains and regardless of the dialogue's purpose, e.g., attestation or service invocation. This zero trust-compliant approach requires each agent to prove ownership of its DID and to present supporting VCs to the other party. The VCs must be cryptographically bound to the DID under investigation. During this exchange, both agents alternate between the roles of a VC holder and a VP verifier: the holder presents its DID and VCs in the form of a VP, while the verifier checks the validity and issuer trustworthiness. If both parties approve the validity of each other's VPs, they are mutually authenticated respectively established trust among each other. At deployment, an agent receives basic (bVCs) or rich VCs (rVCs), depending on its initial role. bVCs encode only minimal information, such as the fact that the entity is an agent, without specifying roles, attributes, capabilities, or authorizations. They are only issued by the security domain's orchestrator. Hence, a bVC contains the orchestrator's DID as the issuer's identifier. While the orchestrator holds its own DID outside the ledger, its DID doc with its verification material is made available to all agents within its security domain. The purpose of bVCs is to empower freshly-deployed agents to trustfully identify themselves to peers of the same security domain in order to receive rVCs. The latter specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent. Obtaining rVCs after deployment involves an intra-domain attestation process. For this, a freshly-deployed agent approaches a designated authority agent of the same security domain that is in charge to equip agents with rVCs. Section: 2 Fundamentals

As introduced by the W3C, DIDs and VCs are central building blocks of the self-sovereign identity (SSI) paradigm (Toth and Anderson-Priddy, 2019). SSI
is an identity model that shifts control of identifiers and credentials from centralized authorities to the individuals that own them, enabling autonomy, privacy preservation, and selective disclosure of information. A DID is a unique, cryptographically verifiable identifier that resolves to a unique DID document (abbr. as DID doc), which specifies public keys, service endpoints, and authentication methods. Since the DID owner possesses the corresponding private keys, it can cryptographically prove ownership of the DID. To ensure integrity and global availability, DID docs are typically anchored in distributed ledgers or other decentralized infrastructures. VCs complement DIDs by enabling third parties to express claims in a signed, tamper-evident format about a subject. The latter is in the claim referred to by its DID. VCs are ideally stored locally by the claim's subject and are shared with others only on demand in the form of a Verifiable Presentation (VP), giving the subject finegrained control over disclosure. SSI defines three roles: issuers, who create, sign and issue VCs; holders and often referred to as the DID subjects, who control and selectively present them as VPs; and verifiers, who validate the integrity and authenticity of a given VP and the trustworthiness of the issuer of the contained VC. As autonomy and privacy-preservation become essential properties of agents operating across organizational boundaries, DIDs and VCs provide a robust foundation for secure, interoperable, and verifiable identity claims.
DIDs and VCs offer several advantages for agents. DID docs do not reveal the agent's identity since they contain no identity attributes. This makes them an ideal artifact to be shared via a commonly accessible ledger. Moreover, in combination with the latter, agents can securely and trustfully update the cryptographic binding of their DIDs to their public keys, e.g., to rotate keys for security purposes, without involving any issuer such as a certificate authority in conventional public key infrastructures. The concept also permits declaring deputies in the DID doc, which allows encoding and enforcing complex human-toagent and agent-to-agent owner relationships (Rodriguez Garzon et al., 2025). Furthermore, VCs are highly flexible and tamper-proof containers for a wide range of claims, making them suitable for carrying human-to-agent and agent-to-agent delegations.

Section: 3 Related Work

Equipping agents with DIDs and VCs has recently attracted significant attention as a foundation for secure and privacy-preserving identity management in multi- agent ecosystems. Chaffer et al. (Chaffer et al., 2024) present the ETHOS framework, which adopts the SSI paradigm for agents. Their work highlights benefits in terms of privacy preservation, risk classification, and compliance record management. By leveraging decentralized identity technologies, ETHOS mitigates risks associated with data centralization and unauthorized access, while simultaneously supporting regulatory audits and compliance. South et al. (South et al., 2025) discuss mechanisms for authenticated delegation among agents. They investigate the sole use of VCs or in combination with OIDC to identify agents and to share verifiable delegations. The LOKA protocol proposed by Ranjan et al. (Ranjan et al., 2025) introduces a framework for ethically governed agent ecosystems. Central to this design is a Universal Agent Identity Layer that leverages DIDs and VCs to establish interoperable and verifiable agent identities. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2025) propose a zerotrust identity framework built on verifiable agent identities using DIDs and VCs, directly addressing shortcomings of conventional identity and access management systems such as static trust models and limited delegation. Their research highlights how these decentralized mechanisms can create robust, contextsensitive trust and authorization, better suited for dynamic, multi-agent environments. The Agent Network protocol (ANP) also leverages DIDs as a mechanism to uniquely identify agents (Chang et al., 2025). Unlike ledger-based approaches, ANP anchors DIDs in centrally managed web servers, reflecting a pragmatic but less decentralized design choice. The Networked Agents and Decentralized AI (NANDA) index's integration of DIDs and VCs for agents is underpinned by the AgentFacts model, which provides a structured, machine-readable template for representing agent identity and capabilities (Raskar et al., 2025). This approach allows registries and clients to validate agent authenticity, assess reputation, and facilitate dynamic trust evaluation. Other noteworthy contributions include Hossen et al.'s secure communication framework for decentralized agents (Hossen et al., 2025) and Zou et al.'s BlockA2A protocol for secure, verifiable agent-to-agent interoperability (Zou et al., 2025).
In contrast, our approach integrates the VC exchange directly into the A2A protocol. By employing the DIF presentation proof protocol 3 in combination with JSON-LD-encoded VCs on top of A2A, our design extends an existing agent-to-agent interoperability mechanism with built-in trust establishment based on standardized protocols and formats from the domain of decentralized identity management.

To implement mutual authentication protocols for rich Verifiable Credentials (rVCs) across different security domains, agents must follow a structured approach that involves several key steps and components as outlined in the retrieved paper "AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials" (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

1. **Ownership and Control of DIDs**: Each agent must possess its own Decentralized Identifier (DID) and be in control of its associated Verifiable Credentials (VCs). The DIDs are anchored in a distributed ledger that spans multiple security domains, which serves as a cross-domain trust anchor for the agents' DID documents (DID docs) (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

2. **Mutual Authentication Requirement**: When initiating a dialogue, agents must mutually authenticate regardless of whether they belong to the same or different security domains. This process is essential for establishing trust and involves proving ownership of their DIDs and presenting supporting VCs that are cryptographically bound to the DIDs under investigation (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

3. **Role of Verifiable Presentations (VPs)**: During the mutual authentication process, agents alternate roles between VC holders and VP verifiers. The holder presents its DID and VCs in the form of a VP, while the verifier checks the validity and trustworthiness of the issuer of the presented VCs. Successful verification leads to mutual authentication and the establishment of trust between the agents (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

4. **Use of Protocols**: The exchange of VPs required for mutual authentication is carried out using the DIF Presentation Exchange protocol. Additionally, the attestation process relies on the DIF Credential Manifest protocol, which facilitates the issuance and verification of VCs (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

5. **Trust Relationships**: Trust is established based on two roots: the technical root of trust, which is the operation of the ledger, and the organizational root of trust, which pertains to the entities that issued the presented VCs. Agents must trust both the ledger's operation and the issuers of the VCs to successfully authenticate across domains (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

6. **Implementation Considerations**: The paper discusses an experimental setup where agents from different security domains authenticate each other using DIDs and VCs. This setup demonstrates the feasibility of cross-domain mutual authentication but also highlights challenges, such as the reliance on LLMs (Large Language Models) to orchestrate security procedures, which can affect the efficiency and reliability of the authentication process (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

The experimental findings indicate that while the approach is technically feasible, practical implementation may require further refinement to enhance efficiency and reliability.

Section: 7 Conclusion and Future Work

This article presented a concept and an experimental setup in which LLM-based AI agents are equipped with self-controlled, ledger-anchored digital identities based on DIDs and VCs. The approach builds on standards originating from the Web3 ecosystem that were originally conceived as technical foundations for selfsovereign digital identities of natural persons. When applied to AI agents, however, these standards enable secure mutual authentication and the establishment of diverse trust relationships across security domains.
The experimental setup employs the DIF presentation proof protocol together with JSON-LD encoded VCs to enable mutual VP exchange. The communication between agents is realized through the framework's native mechanisms in intra-domain scenarios and through the latest A2A protocol in the interdomain scenario. The issuance of VCs is conducted using the DIF Credential Manifest protocol. Despite being applied only in the intra-domain scenario, the attestation of claims can also be conducted across domains, e.g., to issue cross-domain authorizations in the form of VCs. The intra- and inter-domain verifiability of claims becomes possible by anchoring the required key material of the agents' DIDs in a commonly accessible ledger. Agents capable of issuing VCs were introduced to enable future agents to spawn other agents and equip them with verifiable roles, capabilities, and delegations in the form of VCs.
Trust between two agents is established under the assumption that both parties trust the operation of the ledger (technical root of trust) as well as the entities that issued the presented VCs, namely the other domain's issuer (organizational root of trust). But it remains unresolved how trustworthy issuers are identified and designated, and under what legal framework they can be relied upon. The electronic Identification, Authentication and Trust Services (eIDAS) 12 EU regulation has established a legal framework to determine, monitor, and share lists of trusted issuers. Although aimed at natural persons and legal entities, it could be adapted to AI agents acting on their behalf. Future work should therefore not only address tech- nical integration but also explore governance models and policy frameworks that ensure consistent trust management across heterogeneous agent ecosystems.
12 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2014/910/oj
The experimental setup demonstrates the technical feasibility of the proposed approach but also reveals its limitations once the LLM of an agent is in sole charge to orchestrate security-related procedures. This design decision led to an improvable completion rate for all tested LLMs. It is also the root cause of an increased LLM usage which in turn extends the procedures' duration significantly and results in increased costs. While this design decision helps to gain interesting insights of an LLM as the controller of a security procedure, its practical applicability is at least questionable if only because in one evaluation run both agents agreed to skip the authentication in one direction against the policies stated in the system prompt. input: How do self-sovereign digital identities and verifiable credentials operate within multi-agent systems for trust establishment?
actual_output:
Self-sovereign digital identities (DIDs) and verifiable credentials (VCs) play a crucial role in establishing trust within multi-agent systems, as outlined in the retrieved papers.

1. **Conceptual Framework**: The integration of DIDs and VCs allows AI agents to possess long-lived digital identities that are tamper-proof and flexible. This framework enables agents to engage in dialogues across different domains while establishing trust autonomously (arXiv:2511.02841v2). Each agent is equipped with a unique, ledger-anchored DID and a set of third-party issued VCs, which facilitate authentication and trust establishment at the onset of interactions (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

2. **Trust Establishment Process**: Trust between agents is established through a mutual authentication process that involves the exchange of VCs. Agents present their VCs to prove their identity and the claims associated with their DIDs. This process is essential for both intra-domain and inter-domain interactions, where agents must recognize and trust the issuers of the presented VCs (arXiv:2511.02841v2). The trust model incorporates both technical trust (based on the operation of the ledger) and organizational trust (based on the reliability of the issuer) (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

3. **Dynamic Trust Relationships**: The use of VCs allows agents to issue and verify claims about each other in an unstructured format, such as natural language or images. This capability supports the establishment of dynamic trust relationships without the need for extensive standardization processes across different domains (arXiv:2511.02841v2). The flexibility of VCs enables agents to adapt to various contexts and requirements, enhancing their interoperability.

4. **Limitations and Future Work**: While the experimental setup demonstrates the feasibility of using DIDs and VCs for trust establishment, challenges remain, particularly when the control of security procedures is delegated to the agents' language models (LLMs). This can lead to inefficiencies and potential security risks (arXiv:2511.02841v2). Future work is suggested to explore governance models and policy frameworks that ensure consistent trust management across heterogeneous agent ecosystems (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

5. **Related Work**: Other frameworks, such as ETHOS and the LOKA protocol, also leverage DIDs and VCs to enhance privacy, compliance, and trust in agent ecosystems. These frameworks highlight the growing recognition of decentralized identity technologies as foundational for secure multi-agent interactions (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

In summary, self-sovereign digital identities and verifiable credentials are integral to establishing trust in multi-agent systems by enabling secure authentication, dynamic trust relationships, and interoperability across different domains. However, further research is needed to address the limitations of current implementations and to develop robust governance frameworks.

input: What role does the NgramRL system play in enhancing RL post-training via n-gram caching?
actual_output:
The NgramRL system plays a crucial role in enhancing reinforcement learning (RL) post-training by utilizing a rollout-aware n-gram caching mechanism. This approach addresses the high computational costs associated with rollout generation during RL post-training, particularly in the context of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [arXiv:2610.32881v1].

### Key Contributions of NgramRL:

1. **N-gram Cache Utilization**: NgramRL maintains a per-prompt n-gram cache built from prior rollouts of the same prompt. This cache allows the system to propose draft continuations based on previously generated outputs, effectively leveraging the temporal locality of prompts. As noted in the paper, across consecutive epochs, prior rollouts can cover 48-96% of later rollouts, indicating significant redundancy that NgramRL exploits [arXiv:2610.32881v1].

2. **Draft-and-Verify Mechanism**: During each training step, NgramRL proposes draft tokens from the n-gram cache, which are then verified by the policy in a single forward pass. This mechanism ensures that the proposed drafts are aligned with the evolving policy, as the cache is populated with the policy's own outputs, preventing it from becoming stale [arXiv:2610.32881v1].

3. **Efficiency in Resource Usage**: The design of NgramRL allows it to operate without adding persistent GPU memory or requiring auxiliary model training. The cache resides in host memory and is queried on the CPU, which overlaps with GPU computation, thereby minimizing the additional GPU time required for drafting [arXiv:2610.32881v1].

4. **Adaptive Prefetching**: NgramRL incorporates an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that speculatively prepares drafts for likely verification outcomes. This prefetching mechanism helps to keep the cache off the critical path of decoding, allowing for faster processing and reducing the overall time spent on rollouts [arXiv:2610.32881v1].

5. **Performance Improvements**: The implementation of NgramRL has shown significant performance improvements, committing 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward, which is up to 1.99 times more than traditional SuffixDecoding methods and 7.0 times more than prompt-lookup decoding. Additionally, the prefetcher can deliver up to 1.38 times the measured rollout speedup compared to synchronous execution [arXiv:2610.32881v1].

### Conclusion

In summary, NgramRL enhances RL post-training by effectively utilizing n-gram caching to reduce computational costs, improve efficiency, and maintain alignment with the evolving policy. Its innovative draft-and-verify mechanism, combined with adaptive prefetching, allows for significant acceleration in rollout generation while preserving the accuracy and convergence of the training process. This makes NgramRL a valuable optimization in RL-style setups where prompts recur [arXiv:2610.32881v1].

input: How does NgramRL's adaptive n-gram caching compare to traditional methods in optimizing RL post-training?
actual_output:
NgramRL introduces a novel approach to optimizing reinforcement learning (RL) post-training through its adaptive n-gram caching mechanism, which significantly differs from traditional methods. Here are the key insights and findings regarding how NgramRL's approach compares to conventional techniques:

1. **Model-Free Drafter**: Unlike traditional speculative decoding methods that often rely on separate draft models with additional trainable parameters, NgramRL employs a model-free drafter. This drafter is constructed entirely from recent policy rollouts, allowing it to adaptively generate drafts without the need for auxiliary models or persistent GPU memory (NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding, arXiv:2610.32881v1).

2. **Temporal Locality Utilization**: NgramRL leverages prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL rollouts. It recognizes that GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) frequently revisits the same prompts, leading to high overlap in the outputs generated across training epochs. This redundancy is exploited by maintaining a per-prompt n-gram cache that builds on prior rollouts, which is not a characteristic of traditional methods that do not adapt to the evolving policy (NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding, arXiv:2610.32881v1).

3. **Efficiency and Speedup**: The implementation of NgramRL results in substantial efficiency gains. It commits between 3.60 to 7.77 tokens per target-model forward, achieving up to 1.99 times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0 times more than prompt-lookup decoding. This performance is attributed to the adaptive fan-out prefetcher that prepares drafts for likely verification outcomes, effectively hiding host time and maximizing GPU utilization (NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding, arXiv:2610.32881v1).

4. **Lossless Operation**: NgramRL maintains a lossless operation during the decoding process. It ensures that the accepted prefix and bonus tokens remain unchanged, which preserves the output distribution. This contrasts with some traditional methods that may introduce variability or require additional adjustments to maintain output fidelity (NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding, arXiv:2610.32881v1).

5. **Integration and Generality**: NgramRL can be integrated into existing RL frameworks without requiring changes to the reward model, optimizer, or policy architecture. This drop-in optimization capability allows it to complement existing rollout-efficiency methods, making it versatile compared to traditional methods that may require more extensive modifications (NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding, arXiv:2610.32881v1).

In summary, NgramRL's adaptive n-gram caching mechanism offers a more efficient, flexible, and effective approach to optimizing RL post-training compared to traditional methods, which often rely on fixed models and do not adapt to the dynamic nature of RL training.

Traditional speculative-decoding methods often require additional GPU resources and can become misaligned with evolving policies, leading to lower acceptance rates. In contrast, NgramRL maintains a per-prompt n-gram cache that adapts to the policy's changes without retraining, ensuring high-quality draft proposals. Additionally, it employs an adaptive fan-out prefetcher to overlap CPU cache lookups with GPU verification, reducing idle time and improving overall efficiency. This approach allows NgramRL to preserve the output distribution while minimizing training costs, making it a more effective solution for structured generation tasks.

Section: 2.2 Related Work

Model-based speculative decoding. Speculative decoding [3, 10] pairs a fast drafter with the target, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel while preserving the target's output distribution. Strong methods train the drafter as a separate draft model, additional decoding heads such as Medusa [2], or feature-level draft models such as EAGLE [12]. The crucial difference between this literature and our work is that these drafters add trainable parameters and assume a fixed target. In RL post-training both assumptions fail, since the parameters consume scarce GPU memory and a fixed drafter cannot track a policy that changes every step.
Model-free drafters. A separate line copies previously seen tokens rather than predicting them. Prompt-lookup decoding [18] matches 𝑛 -grams against the current prompt, REST [7] retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore, and Token Recycling [14] reuses candidates discarded during a single decode. The closest work is SuffixDecoding [16], which caches token sequences from prior outputs in CPU-side suffix trees and performs best on structured tasks such as text-to-SQL. We operate inside RL training, where the policy is non-stationary and the repetition arises from GRPO revisiting the same prompts. Structured generation. The highest-value targets for RL posttraining, including text-to-SQL, code generation, and tool and API calls, produce outputs with strong syntactic regularity. Completions of the same prompt share schema tokens, keywords, and boilerplate, so identical tokens recur, and copy-based drafting is known to favor such low-entropy outputs [16]. input: How does Link-CBF's per-link clearance guidance compare to Joint-CBF's whole-body safety approach in enhancing robot evasion?
actual_output:
Link-CBF (Link Control Barrier Function) and Joint-CBF (Joint Control Barrier Function) represent two different approaches to enhancing robot evasion in the context of humanoid dodgeball, each with distinct mechanisms and effectiveness based on the available perception.

1. **Link-CBF**: This approach focuses on per-link clearance guidance, which means it assesses the safety of each individual body link (e.g., arms, legs, torso) in relation to potential threats, such as a thrown ball. The Link-CBF reward structure encourages the robot to maintain clearance for every body link, rather than just the pelvis. This method has been shown to improve the robot's success rate significantly, achieving a success rate of 90% in the reset regime and 89% in the deployment regime when using a fixed camera (arXiv:2607.28623v1). The advantage of Link-CBF is that it remains effective even with limited perception capabilities, such as a fixed onboard camera, which only provides depth information.

2. **Joint-CBF**: In contrast, Joint-CBF employs a whole-body safety approach that considers the robot's entire joint configuration. This method requires more accurate perception of the environment, specifically the state of the ball, to effectively guide the robot's evasive maneuvers. While Joint-CBF can theoretically provide stronger safety guarantees, its performance degrades significantly under conditions where the perception is limited. For instance, when using a fixed camera, the success rate drops to 76% in the deployment regime, indicating that the policy struggles to internalize the whole-body barrier effectively without accurate ball state information (arXiv:2607.28623v1).

3. **Comparison and Insights**: The findings suggest that Link-CBF is more robust in scenarios with limited perceptual information, as it successfully extends safety guidance to all body links and achieves higher success rates compared to Joint-CBF under similar conditions. The performance of Joint-CBF improves sharply with better observability of the ball, indicating that its effectiveness is heavily reliant on accurate perception (arXiv:2607.28623v1). Therefore, the choice between Link-CBF and Joint-CBF should be informed by the available sensory data: Link-CBF is preferable when perception is constrained, while Joint-CBF can be advantageous when accurate state information is accessible.

In summary, Link-CBF enhances robot evasion by providing per-link clearance guidance that is effective even with limited perception, while Joint-CBF requires accurate ball state information to function optimally, highlighting the importance of matching the safety structure to the available perceptual capabilities.
expected_output: Link-CBF's per-link clearance guidance improves robot evasion by extending safety measures to every body link, resulting in higher success rates compared to the Joint-CBF approach, especially when perception is limited. In scenarios with a fixed camera, Link-CBF achieved a success rate of 90% in reset and 89% in deployment, while Joint-CBF dropped to 76% in deployment. This suggests that Link-CBF is more effective under conditions where the robot cannot accurately perceive the whole-body barrier, as it focuses on the most immediate threats to limbs rather than relying on a comprehensive whole-body safety structure that may not be accurately perceived.

input: Analyze how advanced sensory feedback and CBFs collaboratively improve evasive maneuvers in humanoid dodgeball.
actual_output:
The collaboration between advanced sensory feedback and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) significantly enhances evasive maneuvers in humanoid dodgeball, as demonstrated in the PAC-MAN framework. This framework integrates perception-aware safety mechanisms with CBFs to enable humanoid robots to react effectively to incoming threats, such as a dodgeball, while maintaining balance.

1. **Role of Sensory Feedback**: The PAC-MAN framework utilizes a head-mounted depth camera to provide the robot with critical information about the incoming ball. This sensory feedback is essential for the robot to perceive the threat and determine which body links are at risk of contact. The depth camera allows the robot to segment the ball and mask the depth image, creating a compact observation that informs the evasive actions (PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball, arXiv:2607.28623v1). The ability to process this information quickly is crucial, as the robot must react within a fraction of a second to avoid contact.

2. **Integration of CBFs**: CBFs provide a structured approach to ensuring safety during evasive maneuvers. They encode collision-free sets and correct unsafe commands based on the robot's state. In the context of dodgeball, the CBFs are designed to guide the robot's movements to avoid contact with the ball while preserving balance (PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball, arXiv:2607.28623v1). The framework employs two levels of CBFs: Link-CBF, which offers lightweight per-link rewards during training, and Joint-CBF, which provides a stronger whole-body joint-space projection that can be used during both training and deployment.

3. **Impact on Evasive Maneuvers**: The combination of sensory feedback and CBFs allows the robot to internalize safety structures that are responsive to its perception of the environment. The study found that the performance of the evasive maneuvers is highly dependent on the quality of the sensory input. For instance, the Joint-CBF performs best when accurate ball states are available, while the Link-CBF is more effective under limited perception conditions (PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball, arXiv:2607.28623v1). This indicates that the robot's ability to evade the ball is enhanced when it can accurately perceive the ball's position and trajectory.

4. **Adversarial Motion Prior**: To further refine the evasive maneuvers, the PAC-MAN framework incorporates an adversarial motion prior (AMP) that regularizes the robot's movements. This motion prior encourages the robot to adopt human-like evasive actions such as crouching, leaning, and sidestepping, which are more effective than arbitrary joint movements (PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball, arXiv:2607.28623v1). The AMP is trained using a discriminator that distinguishes between policy-generated transitions and those from a reference set of human-derived motions, thereby promoting naturalistic evasive behaviors.

In conclusion, the PAC-MAN framework illustrates how advanced sensory feedback and CBFs work together to enhance the safety and effectiveness of evasive maneuvers in humanoid dodgeball. The integration of real-time perception with structured safety mechanisms allows humanoid robots to respond dynamically to fast-moving threats while maintaining balance, ultimately improving their performance in safety-critical scenarios.

Section: B. Related Work

Motion imitation and priors for humanoid control. Motion imitation has long provided a practical route to naturalistic, high-dimensional control. [12] showed that RL can track reference motions reliably, [13] replaced explicit tracking with an adversarial discriminator over motion features, which yields a style reward compatible with a task objective, and [14], [15] learned reusable skill and style embeddings over large motion datasets. These build on a broader body of legged learning [16]-[18] trained from task rewards, command tracking, and domain randomization. Recent wholebody tracking systems move closer to our humanoid setting:
[19] investigates dexterous whole-body control, [20] uses optimized trajectories to train policies, and [5] constructs a standardized whole-body imitation training pipeline. Retargeting quality also matters here, both for general humanoid tracking [21] and for interaction-preserving loco-manipulation [22]. For dodgeball, a motion prior is attractive because the reward for 'not being hit' is too semantically sparse and geometric to specify how a humanoid should move. We select human dodging motions as priors and also condition the policy on a perception stream, thus combining the motion prior with exteroceptive information to produce whole-body evasive reflexes.

PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball

Section: Perception-aware safety, parkour, and fast-object tasks.

The closest conceptual neighbor to perception-aware dodgeball is safe agility under partial exteroception. Quadruped parkour [23], [24] and agile-but-safe locomotion [8] show how perception, skill selection, recovery, and safety layers can support fast motion around obstacles, while humanoid parkour and perception-aware locomotion systems [2], [25][27] extend this to higher-dimensional bodies with depthor elevation-conditioned policies for jumping, leaping, and terrain traversal. Related work studies the same perception-speed-stability tradeoff through depth conditioning [7], online policy switching [28], and active gaze [29]. Dodgeball differs from these terrain-centered settings because the hazard is a fast-moving object rather than traversable terrain. The ball may be visible only briefly, so the policy must forecast imminent body contact and produce an evasive whole-body response instead of merely choosing footholds. Task-centered fast-object work makes this timing pressure explicit: [30] uses humanoid table tennis to study sub-second ball prediction, task planning, and whole-body RL control. Dodgeball shares the timing but changes the objective from striking to avoiding contact. This shift stresses egocentric observability: an onboard depth camera must provide enough information for the body to leave the ball's path before impact.
Whole-body avoidance and safety. Reactive safety spans both recovering balance after a disturbance via capture-point and push-recovery control [31], [32], and avoiding contact in the first place via control barrier functions [10], collisionfree MPC [33], and fast collision-free motion generation [34]. Most related to our safety treatment, [11] injects safety structure during humanoid training and removes the runtime filter at deployment, and [9] concurrently explores egocentric tactile and proximity sensing as a modality complementary to the vision used here. We study depth-based dodgeball on the Unitree G1, using perception-aware CBF-RL to couple onboard visual observations with per-link safety guidance and motion-regularized whole-body evasion.

Section: II. SAFETY-CRITICAL PERCEPTION-AWARE DODGEBALL

We formulate perception-aware dodgeball as a safetycritical whole-body reaction problem under partial observation. The robot must avoid contact with an incoming object while preserving balance, yet its deployed policy has only limited onboard sensing. This information constraint affects both which safety mechanisms we can use and how we measure success.

PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball

Abstract: We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBF-RL framework that couples control-barrier safety with deployment-realistic onboard sensing for whole-body humanoid dodgeball. The deployed policy sees the ball only as segmentation-masked depth from a head-mounted camera, while training-time CBF guidance represents clearance to every body link, and an adversarial motion prior regularizes the resulting evasive reflexes. We evaluate on a controlled any-link contact benchmark with seeded throws in two regimes: single throws and a deployment loop in which the robot walks back to its station and recovers between throws. On this benchmark, the policy comes within a few points of a privileged state oracle: a fixed onboard camera alone is adequate for evasion. We find that usable barrier structure depends on perceptual observability: Joint-CBF gives the best performance with accurate ball states, degrades under fixed-camera observations when used only as training guidance, and recovers with a ball-tracking gimbal or privileged runtime filter. We therefore deploy a lightweight Link-CBF policy zero-shot on the Unitree G1 in the real world, where it tolerates imperfect perception, succeeds on 95% of throws, and uses semantic segmentation to dodge different balls.

PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball

Section: I. INTRODUCTION

Humanoid robots operating around moving objects must react within a fraction of a second, and the evasion itself must not cost them their balance. Dodgeball isolates this safety problem in a short-horizon, whole-body setting: the robot must perceive an incoming ball, determine which links are threatened, and coordinate the torso, arms, and legs quickly enough to avoid contact while remaining upright. Humans solve the same problem by keeping their eyes on the ball and moving their whole body out of its path. Recent learning-based controllers can produce dynamic humanoid locomotion [1], [2], whole-body imitation [3]-[5], and visually conditioned skills [6], [7], but reactive whole-body safety from onboard vision remains difficult [8], [9], especially for a humanoid.
Control barrier functions (CBFs) encode collision-free sets and correct unsafe commands, provided the relevant state is available [10]. Onboard perception breaks this convenient assumption: the incoming object may be visible only briefly, may leave the camera field of view, or may appear as a few noisy depth pixels. CBF-RL can move barrier information into policy training [11], but a deployed policy can internalize only as much safety structure as its observations support. The threat representation and the barrier design therefore

We study this coupling through perception-aware humanoid dodgeball (Fig. 1). A ball is launched toward a humanoid robot, which must avoid contact with every body link and preserve balance using only proprioception and onboard depth at deployment. Unlike navigation around a mapped obstacle, the hazard is transient, and the robot has no nominal velocity command or reference motion that specifies when and how to evade. The short observation window and whole-body collision geometry make dodgeball a direct test of safety under partial observation.
We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBF-RL framework for humanoid dodgeball. The central question is how much barrier structure a policy can internalize when it receives only deployment-realistic observations. PAC-MAN studies two levels: Link-CBF, a lightweight per-link reward used during training, and Joint-CBF, a stronger whole-body joint-space projection that can either guide training or stay active at test time as a privileged runtime filter. The two levels separate learned barrier-guided behavior from online barrier enforcement.
How well the learned reflex works depends on what perception tells the policy about the threat. The deployed system segments the ball in RGB and masks the depth image down to a compact ball-only observation. An active gimbal, studied in simulation, tests whether keeping the threat in view for longer makes the stronger barrier structure usable. An adversarial motion prior (AMP) regularizes how the humanoid moves, so the evasions come out as crouches, leans, sidesteps, and leaps; the safety structure itself comes from the CBF terms.
We use a controlled, contact-based benchmark to ask three questions: whether barrier guidance improves wholebody avoidance, how much barrier structure a policy can internalize without a runtime filter, and how the available perception changes the answer. The benchmark calibrates on-target throws against a frozen statue and covers both single throws and a deployment loop in which the robot walks back to its station and recovers between throws. Across a privileged state oracle, a fixed onboard camera, and an oracle-aimed active gimbal, we find that stronger barrier structure needs more informative observations. The full JointCBF with runtime filtering is strongest when accurate ball states are available, whereas the lighter Link-CBF is the best deployable option under limited onboard perception. We validate this design choice by deploying the fixed-camera Link-CBF policy zero-shot on a Unitree G1 using only onboard depth and proprioception.

We therefore add an adversarial motion prior (AMP) [13] as a motion regularizer. The critical factors influencing cost-aware abstention in IT ticket routing methodologies, as discussed in the retrieved paper "Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification" (arXiv:2610.31657v1), can be summarized as follows:

1. **Cost Structure**: The methodology is heavily influenced by the asymmetric cost structure associated with routing decisions. The costs are categorized into three types: 
   - **c_ok**: Cost of a correct auto-route (illustratively set to 0).
   - **c_triage**: Cost of human triage (illustratively set to 1).
   - **c_wrong**: Cost of an incorrect auto-route (illustratively set to 5).
   This cost structure indicates that misrouting a ticket is significantly more expensive than human triage, which motivates the need for a cost-aware abstention policy (Section A).

2. **Classifier Performance**: The effectiveness of the routing policy is contingent upon the performance of the classifiers used. The paper compares four trained classifiers with four large language models (LLMs) under zero- and few-shot prompting conditions. The results show that a calibration-selected TF-IDF + logistic regression policy can significantly reduce costs and misroutes, highlighting the importance of classifier selection and calibration in cost-aware abstention (Section VII).

3. **Calibration and Confidence Estimation**: The paper emphasizes the importance of calibration in the decision-making process. Many modern classifiers, including LLMs, tend to produce high confidence values that do not correlate well with actual accuracy. The study employs expected calibration error (ECE) and other metrics to assess the reliability of confidence estimates, which are crucial for determining when to trust automated decisions (Section I).

4. **Threshold Selection**: The routing policy is determined by a threshold that is selected based on calibration data. The paper discusses how organizations must estimate their own costs to set appropriate routing thresholds, which directly impacts the effectiveness of the abstention policy (Section III).

5. **Empirical Evaluation Framework**: The authors propose a reproducible empirical framework that separates prediction, confidence, rejection, and cost into distinct stages. This allows for a more nuanced analysis of the assumptions underlying the routing decisions and facilitates future evaluations under similar protocols (Section VII).

6. **Sensitivity Analysis**: The paper includes a post-hoc sensitivity analysis that examines various cost parameters, indicating that the conclusions drawn from the routing policies are contingent upon the specific cost assumptions made by an organization (Section III).

In conclusion, the critical factors influencing cost-aware abstention in IT ticket routing methodologies include the asymmetric cost structure of routing decisions, the performance and calibration of classifiers, the selection of appropriate thresholds, and the establishment of a reproducible evaluation framework. These elements collectively inform the decision-making process regarding when to route tickets automatically and when to defer to human triage.

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: I. INTRODUCTION

Enterprise IT service desks process tens of thousands of internal tickets per month, where the 'customer' is an employee asking internal IT for help with hardware, access, or software (not an external consumer). HDI/MetricNet reports the North American average cost per voice IT service-desk ticket at US$17.19, with walk-up tickets averaging US$37.52 [1]. Routing happens under an asymmetric cost structure. Sending a ticket to the correct queue is nearly free. Sending it to a human triager is moderately costly. Sending it to the wrong queue is much more expensive once you account for handoff latency, double work, and missed service levels. Accuracy or macro-F1 alone cannot represent this asymmetry or indicate when to trust an automated decision [2], [3].
Two trends make this gap more pressing. First, large language models (LLMs) can be prompted as zero- or few-shot text classifiers [4], [5], potentially reducing the need for taskspecific training. Second, modern neural classifiers, including LLMs, are known to be poorly calibrated. They often produce high confidence values regardless of actual accuracy [6]-[9]. Together these trends raise a concrete operational question: should a prompted LLM be allowed to auto-route IT tickets, and if so, under what abstention policy?
We study this question on the public IT Service Ticket Classification Dataset (47,837 tickets, eight categories). We treat cost-aware abstention not as a way to improve a classifier but as an empirical readiness test under stated assumptions. Predictors, confidence estimators, rejection scores, and policies remain separate. Our contributions are:
A comparison of four trained non-LLM classifiers and eight prompted LLM conditions on the same public corpus, including a common 1,000-ticket test subset.
A calibration analysis that reports expected calibration error (ECE), correctness area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and tie-aware area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), plus separate mixed ( M =9 ) and LLM-only ( M =8 ) agreement pools.
A calibration-selected, paired-bootstrap cost analysis with top-probability, probability-margin, and entropy rejection scores; a post-hoc 16-setting cost-parameter analysis; and LLM policies that use a cost-derived threshold rather than test tuning.
A reproducible evaluation framework and per-ticket artifacts that expose prediction, confidence, rejection, and cost as separately auditable stages.
The main observation is simple: abstention does not repair a weak classifier. It exposes when auto-routing is cost-preferred under a particular dataset, confidence signal, and cost model.
Positioning. The components we combine are individually established: Chow-style error-reject [3], Elkan-style costsensitive decision-making [10], ECE-based calibration diagnostics [6], [11], isotonic recalibration, and self-consistencyinspired agreement signals [12]. We introduce no new abstention algorithm. This paper's contribution is an empirical evaluation of deployment-relevant assumptions and its reproducible implementation, not a universal readiness certificate.

Section: II. RELATED WORK

Selective prediction and abstention. The classical framework for rejecting uncertain inputs traces back to Chow's error-reject trade-off [3]. It has been formalized for modern classifiers under the names selective prediction [2], [13] and learning with abstention [14]; a recent survey organizes LLM abstention methods, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics [15]. The closest line is learning to defer , where a classifier is trained jointly with the option to pass an instance to a human expert [16], [17]. Our training-free confidence-threshold policy addresses the same route-or-defer action space without joint training. We evaluate its decisions under an explicit cost model following Elkan's cost-sensitive formulation [10].
Calibration and overconfidence. Guo et al. [6] documented systematic overconfidence in deep neural classifiers and popularized Expected Calibration Error (ECE) [11] as a diagnostic. A growing literature studies whether LLMs are well-calibrated [7]-[9], [18]. The broad finding is that verbalized confidence runs too high. We contribute a publicdataset measurement of LLM ECE in an asymmetric-cost classification setting, and report agreement-across-predictors as a confidence signal inspired by self-consistency [12].
LLMs for text classification. Off-the-shelf prompting of LLMs as classifiers [4], [5], [19] is operationally attractive, but on short, lexical-signal-heavy tasks strong classical text classifiers such as linear SVMs [20] remain highly competitive, as our IT-ticket results confirm (§V-A).
